title: Compilation of the Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa'
summary: The medieval Brethren of Purity compile their vast philosophical-scientific encyclopedia, the Rasa'il -- the direct namesake and inspiration for Ibn Turka's own "New Brethren of Purity" circle roughly 450 years later, and part of the same tradition behind the Ghayat al-hakim / Picatrix.
source: RESEARCH_BRIEF.md, "Cosmology and core concepts"; standard dating for the historical Ikhwan al-Safa'

title: Life of Ibn 'Arabi
summary: The Andalusian "Supreme Master" Ibn 'Arabi lives and writes. Ibn Turka credits him, alongside Sa'd al-Din Hamuya, as one of lettrism's two co-founders after 'Ali -- the two named sources anchoring the entire Investigations project.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2025

title: Death of Ahmad al-Buni
summary: Ahmad ibn 'Ali al-Buni dies, having compiled the Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra -- the most widely copied Arabic magical handbook in history, systematizing the occult properties of the 28 Arabic letters and the 99 Names of God into a cosmological system Ibn Turka's own lettrism draws on two centuries later.
source: OCCULTIMGDB registry record (shams_al_maarif work entry), citing Savage-Smith 2004

title: Death of Sa'd al-Din Hamuya
summary: Hamuya, described in the sources as Ibn 'Arabi's "Iranian twin," dies. Ibn Turka is credited as the first to pair Ibn 'Arabi and Hamuya explicitly as lettrism's two co-founders.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2025

title: Birth of Ibn Turka
summary: Sa'in al-Din 'Ali ibn Turka Isfahani is born, almost certainly in Isfahan, in 770/1369, into a family of scholars, philosophers and qadis. The year is derived: Melvin-Koushki works it back from Ibn Turka's own stated age (59) in the Nafsat al-Masdur I, written in 829/1426. He becomes Chief Judge of Isfahan and, per Melvin-Koushki, the foremost occult philosopher of Timurid Iran.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-55 / printed p.34-38; birth year derived from his stated age in Nafsat I; "Prologue to Pythagorean Renaissance" (2025)

title: Temur takes Isfahan; the Turka family goes to Samarkand
summary: Temur takes Isfahan in 789/1387 and massacres most of its inhabitants, but spares the Turka family and takes them to his court at Samarkand. The elder brother Sadr al-Din is appointed qadi there and the judgeship becomes a Turka family office; Ibn Turka, a teenager, continues his studies under his brother, alongside Qazizada Rumi, until he leaves c. 1393. So his formation begins in Samarkand, not Cairo. None of the later papers mentions these years.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-63 / printed p.34-46; the later papers are silent on Samarkand (claim CL-0712)

title: Fifteen years abroad: Mecca and Cairo
summary: At his brother's insistence, and because conditions in Iran were too strait to carry on the family's philosophical and mystical legacy, Ibn Turka leaves Samarkand c. 1393 (Sharaf al-Din Yazdi is said to go with him) on some fifteen years of study abroad, c. 1393-1408; the dates are Melvin-Koushki's conjecture. He is reported in Mecca and Baghdad, but Cairo leaves the deepest imprint: he studies hadith under Siraj al-Din al-Bulqini (d. 1403) and becomes a disciple of Sayyid Husayn Akhlati, a lettrist, alchemist and geomancer at the court of Sultan Barquq who is the hub of a network the circle calls the "New Brethren of Purity," consciously invoking the medieval Ikhwan al-Safa'. (An earlier version of this timeline put his formation in Cairo 'c. 1390-1397'; the dissertation places the Cairo years inside a c. 1393-1408 absence and his youth in Samarkand.)
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-68 / printed p.34-51; departure and Yazdi's company are conjectured

title: Death of Sayyid Husayn Akhlati
summary: Ibn Turka's Cairo master dies in 799/1397, about four years into Ibn Turka's c. 1393-1408 absence -- so the two overlapped for at most about four years, not the decade a Cairo formation 'c. 1385-1397' would imply. Akhlati's network had radiated from Cairo to Iran, India, and Anatolia -- the connective tissue of Ibn Turka's later intellectual world.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-54 / printed p.34-37

title: Death of Timur
summary: Timur (Temur) dies at Utrar in 807/1405; Ibn Turka learns of it while still abroad. A succession struggle among his sons and grandsons follows -- the Timurid princely rivalries (Pir-Muhammad, Iskandar, Shah Rukh, Baysunghur) that form the setting of Ibn Turka's return to Iran.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-69 / printed p.34-52; Timeline A.1

title: Returns to Isfahan
summary: After about fifteen years abroad Ibn Turka returns to Isfahan, perhaps in 1408-9 ('perhaps two or three years' after Temur's death), and takes up teaching, intending a retired life of contemplation. The date is Melvin-Koushki's conjecture.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-69 / printed p.34-52; return date conjectured

title: Summoned to Pir-Muhammad's court at Shiraz
summary: Pir-Muhammad b. 'Umar-Shaykh summons Ibn Turka to Shiraz and makes him a member of his court -- the first Timurid attachment in the record -- until Pir-Muhammad is murdered in 812/1409 and his brother Iskandar rises in Fars. The dates are conjectured.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-69 / printed p.34-52; summons dates conjectured; the murder is context

title: Ibn Turka joins Iskandar Mirza's court
summary: After Pir-Muhammad's murder (1409) his brother Iskandar Mirza rules Fars, and Melvin-Koushki has Ibn Turka a member of Iskandar's court c. 1409-12, 'presumably' with a teaching post and the judgeship. In 1412-14 Iskandar takes Isfahan and holds a brilliant court there; Ibn Turka, attached to it, moves back to Shiraz because of harassment by envious rivals and proposes a protege as qadi in his place (an inference). Iskandar's atelier fused star science, poetry and manuscript painting; later papers call him Ibn Turka's first patron. The dissertation's own ranges for the court differ (812-15 AH and 815-17 AH).
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.51-69 / printed p.34-52; court dates conjectured; MK '(?)' on the qadi post

title: Fall of Iskandar Sultan
summary: Shah Rukh marches against his nephew Iskandar in 817/1414; Iskandar flees, is captured, blinded and later executed, and his brother Ibrahim Sultan replaces him. Ibn Turka's earlier attachment to Iskandar becomes a liability. (One CE conversion gives 1415 for the same event; the dissertation's timeline gives 817/1414.)
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.52-69 / printed p.35-52; Timeline A.1

title: Attempted retirement from public life
summary: After Iskandar's fall Ibn Turka tries to withdraw from public life for some eight years; he writes the R. Huruf in Shiraz in 1414, 'perhaps for Iskandar' (Melvin-Koushki's own query; a later paper says flatly 'for Iskandar'), and completes a corrected Sharh Fusus al-Hikam in 1415. The span is conjectured.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.52-70 / printed p.35-53; span conjectured; R. Huruf recipient queried by MK

title: Investigations (Kitab al-Mafahis) dated 1420
summary: The master-work, described by Melvin-Koushki as the first fully systematic summa of Islamic lettrism ('ilm al-huruf) -- a mathematical-theurgic philosophy challenging the dominant Aristotelian-Avicennan system of his day -- is dated 823/1420 in its colophon. The date may record copying (taswid) rather than composition: a marginal correction to the autograph colophon in MS Majlis 10196 says so, the day is disputed (1 Sha'ban vs 19 Dhu l-Hijja 823), and the place is given as 'Isfahan or Yazd?'. It was revised and expanded in 828/1425 in the company of Yazdi. The dissertation names no patron; later papers say Iskandar commissioned it, though Iskandar was dead by 1414.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.52 / printed p.35 (Timeline A.1); pdf p.99 / printed p.82 (entry and colophon note); later papers name Iskandar as commissioner (see TurkaVita/docs/TURKA_AUDIT.md section B)

title: Samarkand Observatory founded (later papers' dating)
summary: Ulugh Beg founds his observatory in Samarkand. Four later Melvin-Koushki papers (the Prologue, Sensorium, New Brethren and Timurid-Mughal chapters) date the founding to 1420 and link it to the Mafahis, treating the coincidence as more than decorative: star science and letter science boomed together in this milieu. The dissertation does not date the founding or draw the parallel; it mentions the observatory through Qazizada Rumi as director and through Yazdi's later invitation. It is context for the life, not an event of it.
source: Melvin-Koushki, "Prologue to Pythagorean Renaissance" (2025) and three later papers; the dissertation (Yale 2012) is silent on the date (TurkaVita claim CL-0731)

title: The Tahawi Circle diagram
summary: The Mafahis's central diagram -- called the first "modern" lettrist reworking of the Pythagorean Tetractys -- is a master diagram of the work, which survives in MS Majlis 10196 (the manuscript with Ibn Turka's own hand at ff. 52a and 118b). The single strongest candidate for a curated manuscript image of his actual work.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.353 (the Tahawi Circle as master diagram); Melvin-Koushki 2021, 2025

title: Yazdi and the Mafahis manuscript
summary: Sharaf al-Din 'Ali Yazdi -- Ibn Turka's best friend and foremost student, later a Timurid imperial historian at the Samarkand Observatory -- is tied to the earliest copy of Ibn Turka's masterwork (Tehran, Majlis Library MS 10196). Ff. 52a and 118b are in Ibn Turka's own hand (incipit and explicit); the earliest copies carry a note that Yazdi checked the copy and attended teaching on the work (f. 119a; Beinecke Landberg 146 f. 179b). The Prologue says the hand of ff. 52a-56a is 'almost certainly' Yazdi's; the dissertation does not say so, and Melvin-Koushki's own texts differ on this point (unresolved).
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.95, 97, 99, 116; "Prologue to Pythagorean Renaissance" (2025) for the 'almost certainly' attribution

title: The Baysunghur Qur'an
summary: A monumental illuminated Qur'an produced under Baysunghur's patronage. Ibn Turka's circle's numerological/lettrist framing of manuscript illumination programs makes this exactly the kind of project his doctrine could plausibly have touched.
source: RESEARCH_BRIEF.md, "Courts and political economy"

title: First trial: accused of Sufi bias
summary: Melvin-Koushki writes of "three trials" but never lists them in one place; his timeline and text date them c. 1422, 1426 and 1427. The first: c. 825/1422 Isfahan enemies accuse Ibn Turka at Shah Rukh's court of sufigari (Sufi bias); he travels to Herat, wins Shah Rukh's favour, is offered Isfahan but chooses Yazd, and is given the judgeship there (the account is his own, in Nafsat I, written under duress). Mapping 'the three' onto these dates is this project's reading.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.52-70 / printed p.35-53; the c. 1422 date is conjectured

title: Judge at Yazd
summary: Ibn Turka's years in Yazd, where he holds the judgeship, are productive: students flock to him, by his own report from as far as Shiraz, Samarkand, Anatolia and India, he writes many lettrist works, and the Mafahis is revised and expanded in 1425 with Sharaf al-Din Yazdi. His Yazd enemies' grievance, by 1426, is that he applies the Shari'a impartially.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.52-72 / printed p.35-55; span conjectured; the students are his own report in Nafsat II

title: Baysunghur: addressee and commissioner from 1426
summary: No source dates the start of any patronage by Baysunghur, Shah Rukh's son and a calligrapher-prince (an earlier version of this timeline had 'Ibn Turka enters Baysunghur's court c. 1416', which nothing supports). Baysunghur is appointed governor of Mazandaran and western Khurasan in 1415, while 1414-c. 1422 is an attempted retirement for Ibn Turka. The firm links are later: the R. Su'al al-Muluk, written 'at his request' before 829/1426; the Nafsat al-Masdur II and R. I'tiqadiyya addressed to him c. 1429-32; and his son 'Ala' al-Din as dedicatee of the R. Tuhfa-yi 'Ala'i (1428). Later papers call him Ibn Turka's 'second patron' without a start date.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.52-74 / printed p.35-57; "second patron" is the later papers' label, without a date

title: On the Splitting of the Moon and the Last Hour
summary: Ibn Turka's Persian treatise (R. Shaqq-i Qamar), dated 829/1426 -- a terminus 'before 28 January 1426' (another listing prints 27 February), possibly a copy date -- reads Q 54:1 through a seven-tier hierarchy of knowers: (1) jurists and traditionists, (2) dialectical theologians, (3) peripatetic philosophers, (4) illuminationists, (5) verifying mystics of the Ibn 'Arabi school, (6) lettrists, and (7) 'Ali and the Imams -- though, Melvin-Koushki argues, level seven is 'not entirely what it seems': it is peculiar to the present time and marked by a conjunction, and is not simply the Imams. A three-tier hierarchy (philosophers, Sufis, lettrists) appears in the Sharh-i Nazm al-Durr. Other later papers compress the ladder differently (lettrism at the top; two lettrist levels).
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.332-334 (text), pdf p.471-479 (translation), pdf p.126-128 (date)

title: Second trial: the Yazd delegation
summary: In 829/1426 Yazd elite, angered by his impartial application of the Shari'a, send a delegation to Herat and cite a youthful verse praising 'Ali; Shah Rukh summons him, and Ibn Turka answers with the Nafsat al-Masdur I and a creed tract (R. I'tiqadat), regaining Shah Rukh's favour. Melvin-Koushki writes of 'three trials'; taking this as the second is the project's reading.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.52-75 / printed p.35-58

title: The Nafsat al-Masdur I: an apology under duress
summary: Ibn Turka's defensive apology to Shah Rukh, written 16 May 1426, which is also our source for his stated age (59) and for much of his own account of his career. Melvin-Koushki stresses that the apologies were 'produced under great duress' and are hardly reflective of Ibn Turka's primary concerns: they show what he told a ruler, not necessarily what he held. (The Prologue's remark that he 'refused to bend the knee' at his trials is uncited; the dissertation shows apologies to Shah Rukh in 1426 and to Baysunghur c. 1429-32.)
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.25 (duress), pdf p.55, 72-75 / printed p.38, 55-58; the 16 May date per TurkaVita notes R1/R8

title: Qasim-i Anvar expelled from Herat
summary: The Sufi poet Qasim-i Anvar -- described in a Melvin-Koushki footnote (citing Virani) as Ibn Turka's 'charismatic associate from his Cairo days', and placed with him on a visit to Akhlati by Ni'matullahi hagiography (a low-confidence report) -- is arrested and expelled from Herat in the same 830/1427 purge of suspected Hurufis that catches Ibn Turka, on the strength of a putative Hurufi link.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.73 / printed p.56 and pdf p.53 / printed p.36 (the purge); pdf p.456 / printed p.439, n.16 (Qasim-i Anvar); pdf p.68 / printed p.51 (hagiography)

title: Third trial: the Hurufi purge and exile
summary: In 830/1427 the Hurufi Ahmad-i Lur attempts to kill Shah Rukh outside the congregational mosque in Herat and is killed; those with suspected Hurufi sympathies are arrested or exiled. Recalled to Herat, Ibn Turka is stripped of position and property, tortured and imprisoned, writes to Amir Firuzshah seeking redress, and is then exiled (1427-c. 1430, 'much of the next five years'). Whether this is 'the third' of the trials is the project's reading of Melvin-Koushki's phrase.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.53-73 / printed p.36-56

title: Simnan, Natanz and Sa'in Qal'a
summary: In exile Ibn Turka makes a fruitless attempt to obtain a hearing with Shah Rukh at Simnan (c. 1429 in the timeline, 1430 in the text), winters in Natanz, sends for his family and writes the K. al-Manahij for his son Muhammad, then obtains a hearing at Shah Rukh's camp at Sa'in Qal'a and a promise of reinstatement (1430). The dates are conjectured.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.53-74 / printed p.36-57; Simnan dated c. 1429 in the timeline, 1430 in the text

title: Nine months at Herat
summary: Ibn Turka travels to Herat and for nine months attends court weekly, awaiting review of his case; he writes the Nafsat al-Masdur II and the R. I'tiqadiyya for Baysunghur. The promised review never comes.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.53-74 / printed p.36-57

title: Ibn Turka dies at Herat
summary: After nine months of weekly attendance at court awaiting review of his case, Ibn Turka dies in Herat on Monday 14 Dhu l-Hijja 835 / 12 August 1432, frustrated, impoverished and in limbo. Melvin-Koushki gives his age as 63, though his own dates imply about 65 (a flagged inconsistency). His Mafahis, per Melvin-Koushki, remains understudied -- "on the Index" -- for centuries afterward.
source: Melvin-Koushki, dissertation (Yale 2012), pdf p.53-74 / printed p.36-57

title: Marsilio Ficino is born
summary: One year after Ibn Turka's death, the man who will become the central translator-philosopher of Renaissance Hermeticism in Europe is born in Florence. Not a documented comparison in the sources in hand -- included only as an orienting coincidence of timing.
source: Standard European Renaissance chronology

title: Ulugh Beg's star catalog completed
summary: The Zij-i Sultani, produced at the Samarkand Observatory Ibn Turka's own circle was adjacent to via Yazdi, is completed five years after Ibn Turka's death -- the most accurate pre-telescopic star tables produced, remaining in active use from the Strait of Malacca to London into the 19th century.
source: RESEARCH_BRIEF.md; Melvin-Koushki 2021

title: Nicholas of Cusa, De Docta Ignorantia
summary: Cusa's treatise on "learned ignorance" appears. Melvin-Koushki explicitly compares Ibn Turka to Cusa -- "fellow lawyer, fellow Pythagoreanizer, but far less immediately influential" than Ibn Turka was in his own world.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2025 (comparison); publication date is standard European intellectual history

title: Kashifi's "Everyman's Library" popularizations
summary: Husayn Va'iz Kashifi and his son 'Ali Safi simplify and popularize the same occult-science material Ibn Turka treats with dense, elite difficulty, aiming at a wider, more commercial readership -- a live tension between hoarding prestige and teaching for reach that runs through the whole tradition.
source: RESEARCH_BRIEF.md, "Courts and political economy"

title: Death of Sharaf al-Din 'Ali Yazdi
summary: Ibn Turka's best friend and foremost student -- by then a celebrated Timurid imperial historian working at the Samarkand Observatory -- dies, 22 years after his teacher.
source: RESEARCH_BRIEF.md

title: Ficino translates the Corpus Hermeticum
summary: Commissioned by Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino's Latin translation of the (pseudo-)Hermetic corpus becomes the founding textual act of European Renaissance Hermeticism -- a structurally close parallel to Ibn Turka's own project of systematizing an inherited esoteric-philosophical tradition into a totalizing cosmology, though not a comparison drawn directly in the sources currently in hand.
source: Standard Renaissance-Hermeticism historiography (see Yates 1964, below)

title: Pico della Mirandola, Oration on the Dignity of Man
summary: Pico's Oration and his 900 Theses -- which incorporate Christian Kabbalah alongside Hermeticism and scholastic philosophy -- appear. Melvin-Koushki names Pico directly, alongside Cusa, Bruno, and Dee, as a figure worth reading Ibn Turka against.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2025 (comparison, named directly); dates are standard Renaissance chronology

title: Pico's Theses condemned; disputation blocked
summary: Pope Innocent VIII condemns several of Pico's 900 Theses and blocks the public Rome disputation Pico had planned. A structural echo of Ibn Turka's own inquisitions: a syncretic occult-philosophical system provoking institutional persecution, in a European context roughly contemporary with Ibn Turka's own reception history.
source: Standard Renaissance chronology; the structural parallel to Ibn Turka's inquisitions is this project's own observation, not a claim from the sources in hand

title: 'Ali Safi, Boon for the Khan
summary: A Persian manual of illusionism and trickery (Tuhfa-yi khani) written in 1522 for Durmish Khan Shamlu, the Qizilbash governor of Khurasan -- the 'royal boon' commission language of Melvin-Koushki's The Occult Court belongs to this book, not to Ibn Turka's life -- cataloguing concrete named operations: putrefactions, suffumigations, sleeper interrogation, treasure dowsing, instant agriculture. Real period spellbook texture, translated in full in the paper.
source: Melvin-Koushki, "The Occult Court" (2025), pdf p.3 (a 1522 manual commissioned by a Qizilbash governor)

title: John Dee is born
summary: Born in London. Nearly a century after Ibn Turka's death, Dee becomes the Elizabethan mathematician-magus Melvin-Koushki pairs Ibn Turka against most extensively: "Ibn Turka is best approached as a Timurid Dr. Dee -- or Dee best approached as an Elizabethan Dr. Littleturk."
source: Melvin-Koushki 2021, "Dr Dee's Ottoman Adventure"

title: Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia (full edition)
summary: Cornelius Agrippa's three-book encyclopedic synthesis of natural, celestial, and ceremonial magic reaches its full published form -- Europe's closest analog to the encyclopedic occult-science manuals (like 'Ali Safi's Boon for the Khan) circulating in Ibn Turka's own milieu.
source: Standard European occult-history chronology; not a direct comparison drawn in the sources in hand

title: Giordano Bruno is born
summary: Born in Nola, Kingdom of Naples. Bruno becomes the figure Melvin-Koushki compares Ibn Turka to most extensively and explicitly: both subordinated all contemporary schools of thought to a totalizing Pythagorean/lettrist code, and both were "historiographically burnt at the stake" -- Bruno literally, Ibn Turka's Mafahis left understudied and effectively "on the Index" for centuries.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2025

title: Akbar becomes Mughal emperor
summary: Akbar's reign (1556-1605) is offered by Melvin-Koushki as the most successful avatar of the millennial occult-scientific sovereignty model Ibn Turka's circle helped originate -- syncretizing Muslim, Hindu, Jain, and Christian traditions into what becomes "modern India."
source: Melvin-Koushki 2021

title: Murad III becomes Ottoman Sultan
summary: Murad III's reign (1574-1595) is framed by Melvin-Koushki as that of a Sufi-initiate sultan devoted to oneiromancy, astrology, and talismanry -- a "sister science" to Jewish kabbalah -- who fashioned himself a prophet-saint-king on the strength of personal angelic communications, directly paralleling Dee's own angel-conversations. His reign spans the Islamic millennium (992 AH / 1592 CE).
source: Melvin-Koushki 2021

title: Dee and Kelley's angelic conversations
summary: John Dee and Edward Kelley conduct their scrying sessions, recording conversations with angels including material connected to the garbled "Arabic book" lore (the Book of Soyga) that Melvin-Koushki argues derives from the Bunian-Bistamian magical corpus popular in Ottoman courtly circles -- a direct textual thread from the Islamicate lettrist-talismanic tradition into English angel magic.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2021

title: Safavid New Isfahan built as talismanic architecture
summary: Shah Abbas I's New Isfahan and the Shaykh Lutf Allah Mosque are read by Melvin-Koushki as literal built diagrams of the same Planet-Pearl-Peach cosmology structuring Ibn Turka's Investigations -- cities and buildings as functioning talismans, not merely symbolic ones, nearly two centuries after Ibn Turka's death.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2025

title: Giordano Bruno executed in Rome
summary: Bruno is burned at the stake by the Roman Inquisition. The literal event behind Melvin-Koushki's framing of both Bruno and Ibn Turka as men "historiographically burnt at the stake" for a totalizing occult-scientific system -- one destroyed by fire, the other by centuries of scholarly neglect.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2025 (framing); execution date is standard history

title: John Dee dies in poverty
summary: Dee dies poor, his library destroyed, his repeated bids for imperial patronage in England and the Habsburg lands all having failed -- the real ending Melvin-Koushki's counterfactual "Dr Dee's Ottoman Adventure" imagines Dee escaping by seeking patronage in the more occult-friendly Ottoman court instead.
source: Melvin-Koushki 2021

title: Kristeller, The Philosophy of Marsilio Ficino
summary: Paul Oskar Kristeller's foundational study establishes Renaissance Platonism-Hermeticism as a serious field of modern scholarship in Europe -- decades before comparable systematic attention was paid to the Islamicate occult-scientific tradition Ibn Turka worked in.
source: General Renaissance-studies historiography; not verified against a primary bibliographic record in this project's corpus

title: Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition
summary: Frances Yates's landmark study argues Renaissance Hermeticism -- not just humanism -- was a driving force behind the early Scientific Revolution in Europe. Melvin-Koushki's own "Occult-Scientific Revolution" framing for Ibn Turka's world explicitly writes in the shadow of, and against the geographic limits of, this book's influence.
source: General historiography of Renaissance esotericism; not verified against a primary bibliographic record in this project's corpus

title: Sabra challenges the "decline" narrative of Islamic science
summary: A.I. Sabra's "The Appropriation and Subsequent Naturalization of Greek Science in Medieval Islam" reframes Islamic science as a fully naturalized, ongoing tradition rather than a transmission pipeline that declined after a supposed "golden age" -- part of the historiographical groundwork that makes a claim like Ibn Turka's continued 15th-century scientific vitality legible to later scholars.
source: General historiography of Islamic science; not verified against a primary bibliographic record in this project's corpus

title: Netton, Muslim Neoplatonists
summary: Ian Richard Netton's introduction to the Brethren of Purity's thought becomes a standard English-language reference for the Ikhwan al-Safa' tradition Ibn Turka's own circle explicitly names itself after.
source: IslamicateOccultPortal bibliography (data/seed.json)

title: Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance
summary: George Saliba argues for direct textual transmission from the late Islamic astronomical tradition -- including work connected to the Maragha and Samarkand schools -- into Copernicus's own models, the single strongest historiographical bridge between the world Ulugh Beg's observatory belonged to and the European Scientific Revolution story.
source: General historiography of Islamic science; not verified against a primary bibliographic record in this project's corpus

title: Gardiner on al-Buni's manuscript transmission
summary: Noah Gardiner's "Forbidden Knowledge? Notes on the Production, Transmission, and Reception of the Major Works of Ahmad al-Buni" reconstructs how al-Buni's foundational lettrist-talismanic corpus actually circulated in manuscript -- essential groundwork for tracing the textual lineage feeding into Ibn Turka's own generation.
source: OCCULTIMGDB registry citation record

title: Melvin-Koushki's dissertation on Ibn Turka
summary: Matthew Melvin-Koushki completes his Yale doctoral dissertation, The Quest for a Universal Science, on Ibn Turka's occult philosophy -- the modern scholarly rediscovery this project's research traces back to, and its spine source for the biography (Timeline A.1 and Chapter 1), read page by page. Its dates are the ones the biographical events above rest on.
source: Melvin-Koushki, The Quest for a Universal Science (Yale 2012), held and ingested in TurkaVita (corpus id SRC-610EE1D6BA)

title: "Astrology, Lettrism, Geomancy" article
summary: Melvin-Koushki's "Astrology, Lettrism, Geomancy: The Occult-Scientific Methods of Post-Mongol Islamicate Imperialism" (Medieval History Journal 19.1) lays out the framework -- occult science as literal imperial political technology across the post-Mongol Persianate world -- that the later papers on Ibn Turka specifically build on.
source: Citation recorded in OCCULTIMGDB's shams_al_maarif and persian-astrolabe registry entries

title: "Dr Dee's Ottoman Adventure" published
summary: Melvin-Koushki publishes the counterfactual essay explicitly pairing Ibn Turka and John Dee -- the single richest source in this project's hands for the direct comparative framing between Islamicate and European Renaissance occult philosophy.
source: This project's own bibliography, research/notes/01-dr-dees-ottoman-adventure.md

title: "Prologue to Pythagorean Renaissance" published
summary: Melvin-Koushki's core biographical and cosmological source on Ibn Turka appears, arguing Investigations is the opening anthem of an Islamicate parallel to (and, per the author, a source for) the European Scientific Revolution story.
source: This project's own bibliography, research/notes/02-prologue-to-pythagorean-renaissance.md

title: "The Occult Court" published
summary: Melvin-Koushki's Al-Masaq article lays out the Occult Quintet hierarchy and the patronage economics of the Timurid-to-Safavid occult courts in full, including a complete translation of 'Ali Safi's Boon for the Khan -- this project's core source for court culture and game-mechanical structure alike.
source: This project's own bibliography, research/notes/03-the-occult-court.md
